findings.title: New order() method has no default and breaks external implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider.java adds `int order()` without a default implementation. Every existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider will now fail to compile/link with NoSuchMethodError. The in-tree DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider were updated, but third-party providers were not. Consequence is a breaking API change; it should be a `default` method (e.g. default 0/100) to remain backwards compatible.

findings.title: Multiple crypto providers silently ignored instead of failing
findings.body: detectProvider() in CryptoIntegration.java previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() and silently picks the first, logging only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if e.g. both default and FIPS jars are present the choice among equals is ServiceLoader-order dependent and non-deterministic. Consequence is misconfiguration (notably FIPS vs non-FIPS) is now hidden and the server may run with the wrong crypto stack without any warning.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns unrelated KeyStore provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, typically the JDK SUN provider, and presents it as the BouncyCastle provider. Callers that expect a BC/BCFIPS provider name or BC-specific algorithms via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER will get the wrong provider, causing NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently using a different implementation. A lightweight provider should return null (like WildFlyElytronProvider does) or throw, not a misleading unrelated provider.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion does not validate lengths and silently truncates
findings.body: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java, concatenatedRSToASN1DER() assumes signature.length == signLength without checking and will throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on malformed input instead of IOException. Conversely asn1derToConcatenatedRS()/integerToBytes() truncates when BigInteger is negative or larger than qLength by copying only the low bytes without any check. Consequence is malformed or attacker-controlled DER signatures are silently mapped to a different valid-looking raw R||S value instead of being rejected, which is a signature-parsing integrity risk. Both directions must validate sizes and sign and throw IOException.

findings.title: readSequence accepts indefinite length and trailing garbage
findings.body: ASN1Decoder.readSequence() in ASN1Decoder.java calls readLength() which can return -1 for indefinite-length encoding 0x80, but readSequence() does not reject -1 and will return an empty list, later reported only as size != 2. It also never verifies that the declared sequence length was exactly consumed and that no trailing bytes remain after the sequence. Consequence is malformed DER signatures with indefinite lengths or appended garbage can be accepted into the ECDSA conversion path instead of being strictly rejected as required for DER.

findings.title: Test reuses P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies signature
findings.body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java generates one EC KeyPair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default P-256/secp256r1) in the constructor and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512 tests. The ES384/ES512 cases therefore do not exercise real P-384/P-521 keys and lengths (e.g. 96/132 byte R||S), only zero-padded P-256 values. The test also only checks round-trip rs->DER->rs equality and never verifies the converted DER with Signature.verify() or compares to JCA output. Consequence is the test passes while giving false confidence about interop for larger curves and about correctness of the DER encoding.
